Sir '''Thomas Henry Havelock''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (24 June 1877 – 1 August 1968) was an English applied mathematician, hydrodynamicist and mathematical physicist.<ref>{{acad|id=HVLK897TH|name=Havelock, Thomas Henry}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Binnie | first1 = A. M. | last2 = Roberts | first2 = P. H. | year = 1971 | title = Thomas Henry Havelock. 1877–1968 | journal = Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society | volume = 17 | pages = 327–377 | jstor = 769711 | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1971.0013  | doi-access = free| s2cid = 71812481 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Roberts | first1 = P. H. | year = 1970 | title = Thomas Henry Havelock | journal = Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society | volume = 2 | issue = 2| pages = 221–232 | doi = 10.1112/blms/2.2.221 | doi-access = free }}</ref> He is known for Havelock's law (1907).<ref>Charney, E. (2012). "National Institute of Arthritis, Metabolism and Digestive Diseases, National Institutes of Health." [https://books.google.com/books?id=9kvUBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA213 ''Molecular Electro-Optics: Electro-Optic Properties of Macromolecules and Colloids in Solution''] 64, 213–227</ref><ref name=HavelockLaw>{{cite journal|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=pst.000060051424;view=1up;seq=68|author=Havelock, T. H.|year=1907|title=The Dispersion of Double Refraction in Relation to Crystal Structure|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Containing Papers of a Mathematical and Physical Character|volume=80|issue=535|pages=28–44|doi=10.1098/rspa.1907.0071|bibcode=1907RSPSA..80...28H|doi-access=free}} '''Havelock's Law'''</ref>

Havelock was born in [[Newcastle upon Tyne]]. At the age of sixteen, he entered [[Newcastle University#History|Durham College of Physical Science]]. (Durham College of Physical Science was renamed Armstrong College in 1904.) He matriculated in 1897 at [[St John's College, Cambridge]] and graduated there B.A. in 1900 and M.A. in 1904. From 1903 to 1909 he was a Fellow of St John's College, Cambridge. He was a professor of applied mathematics at Armstrong College from 1914 until his retirement in 1945. (In the 1930s Armstrong College became part of King's College, Durham, which in the 1960s became part of Newcastle University.)

==Havelock's law==
Relationship between the [[refractive index]] <math>n</math> and the wavelength <math>\lambda</math> of a homogeneous material that transmits light:<ref>{{cite book|title=Laws and Models: Science, Engineering, and Technology|author=Hall, Carl W.|chapter=Havelock Law|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EEhpsf6L09gC&pg=PA204|page=204|year=1999|publisher=CRC Press |isbn=9781420050547}}</ref><ref name=HavelockLaw/>
:<math>k = B \ \lambda</math> <math>n</math><math>/{(n-1)^2}</math>, where
::<math>k</math> = constant for the material at a given temperature
::<math>B</math> = [[Kerr constant]] of the material (The Kerr constant is approximately proportional to the absolute temperature.)
::<math>\lambda</math> = wavelength of the material
::<math>n</math> = refractive index of the material

==Awards and honours==
*1914 – F.R.S.
*1956 – William Froude Gold Medal of the [[Royal Institution of Naval Architects]]
*1957 – Knighthood
*1960 - Honorary doctorate from the [[University of Hamburg]]
